rv.q: Yet the drama still hits against the limits of Ibsen's strange and static story: you do not quite know if Solness is to be admired or condemned.
David Edgar’s pensive translation loses the bite and momentum of Ibsen’s dark parable of obsessive ambition
Comprising strong performances with a modern bent, Mehmet Egen’s take on David Edgar’s translation of Ibsen’s The Master Builder is a compelling watch.
There’s a considerable amount to admire in this production , but it is ultimately something of a hollow edifice.
A considerably pacier production would have made for a more engaging evening.
Ergen’s classy production is made by its clarity and focus on the text, using David Edgar’s 2011 adaptation with its direct, casually earthy English.
If timing is everything in live theatre, this production has to be admired for its wonderfully integrated playing.
Now revived at the Arcola in a taut, enthralling production, it manages to unite the figurative and symbolic aspects of this complex play.
It’s still a superb, one might say psychically clean production: the best a rational world can offer.

The power of Ibsen’s play is in the tension between all the oppositions that are sharpened by Mehmet Ergen’s meticulous direction and augmented by our awareness the audience is complicit in all the willing as it anticipates a catastrophic outcome.

Beautifully layered, this text, awash with phallic and psycho-sexual symbolism - how many steeples can you squeeze into one play?— remains a fascinating exploration of human frailty, repressed guilt and buried trauma from modern drama’s very own master builder.
Hicks has created a Master Builder of tragic proportions and Binder's Hilde is the perfect ageing man's fantasy.
Ultimately, The Master Builder succeeds through its compelling performances, above all Binder’s mesmerising and unsettling portrayal of Hilde.

AFTER a slow and rather mannered start, Mehmet Ergen’s production of Ibsen’s The Master Builder (in David Edgar’s adaptation) settles into a tense, beguiling exploration of creative ambition, guilt and the fear of being usurped by the next generation.
While the foundations of this project are strong, the piece in the whole feels a little underpowered and inconsistent in what is certainly a tricky play to mount.
The production works in places but not in others.
Regardless this is a wholly competent production, it has its "4 walls and a roof" but unfortunately does not reach the dizzying heights of greatness.
Put simply, in the pursuit of minimalism, this version of The Master Builder is lacking some essential building blocks to make this a layered version of Ibsen’s classic.
Thought-provoking and anchored by two excellent central performances, The Master Builder is well worth seeing.
A stylish production of The Master Builder, directed by Mehmet Ergen, melds strong performances with striking design.
Its visual symbolism, character contrasts and haunting final scene effectively expose the cost of unchecked pride and soulless ambition.

cn.t: Strong performances, especially from Greg Hicks, anchor this psychologically compelling production, though some find Edgar's adaptation lacks cohesion and the slow pace undermines Ibsen's deeper themes.
